perspective:
From Gloria Bangura’s perspective:

- I work as an administrative assistant at a large event planning company. Donald is a part-time bartender at company events. We’re colleagues but not personally close; we mainly interact during events.
- Over several company events, I noticed Donald seemed distracted and less enthusiastic while serving drinks. I interpreted this as possible unhappiness with his job.
- I approached him and asked if everything was okay with the job. He told me he was “not as into it as I used to be” and that it felt “kind of repetitive.”
- After reflecting on that conversation, I began to suspect his job dissatisfaction might be connected to something deeper. I suggested he consider talking to a professional. He said he hadn’t really thought about it and wasn’t sure it would help.
- After that conversation, I sensed a shift in Donald’s behavior toward me and worried he resented my suggestion as overstepping. I told him I only wanted to help and meant well. He said he was “taken aback at first” but knew I meant well, and that it was “a lot to process.”
- I felt relieved that the tension had eased, and I wanted to strengthen our working relationship. I invited him to collaborate on an upcoming project, saying it could use his creative input. He thanked me and said he appreciated it, wanted to be more involved, and thought it sounded like a great opportunity.
- After the project, I observed Donald’s significant contributions and renewed enthusiasm. I believed he was a valuable team member, so I publicly acknowledged his work in a meeting, saying his efforts were crucial. He thanked me and said the recognition meant a lot to him and that being appreciated felt great.
